content: 1. Momelotinib increases the toxicity of tenofovir alafenamide (AF) due to competition for plasma protein binding. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. 2. Momelotinib, as a BCRP inhibitor, may increase the exposure of BCRP substrates, potentially raising the risk of adverse reactions associated with these substrates. Dose adjustments for other BCRP substrates may be necessary, and close monitoring is advised. 3. Nirmatrelvir increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by altering hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution should be exercised, and close monitoring is recommended. Co-administration may lead to increased systemic exposure to tenofovir. 4. Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. Co-administration may elevate systemic exposure to tenofovir. 5. Orlistat decreases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Caution is required, and close monitoring is recommended. Loss of virological control has been reported in HIV-infected patients taking orlistat concomitantly, possibly due to a drug-drug interaction that inhibits systemic absorption of the antiretroviral drug. HIV RNA levels should be frequently monitored, and orlistat should be discontinued if an increased HIV viral load is confirmed. 6. Otesaconazole increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF through mechanisms involving BCRP inhibition. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is required. Otesaconazole may enhance the effects and toxicities of BCRP substrates. The lowest starting dose of BCRP substrates should be used, or their doses should be reduced. 7. Regorafenib increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by likely inhibiting BCRP (ABCG2) transport. Co-administration with a BCRP substrate may increase systemic exposure to the substrate and related toxicities. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is necessary. 8. Safinamide increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting intestinal BCRP. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is required. BCRP substrates should be monitored for increased pharmacologic or adverse effects. 9. Sarecycline increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution is necessary, and close monitoring is recommended. Toxicities of P-gp substrates may require dosage reductions when co-administered with P-gp inhibitors. 10. Sotorasib decreases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by affecting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Alternative drugs should be used if possible. If unavoidable, refer to the prescribing information of the P-gp substrate for dosage modifications. Close monitoring is essential. 11. Stiripentol increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting BCRP transport. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is required. Dosage reductions for BCRP substrates should be considered if adverse effects occur during co-administration. 12. Tafamidis increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) in vitro, potentially increasing exposure to BCRP substrates following tafamidis or tafamidis meglumine administration. Dosage adjustments for these substrates may be necessary, and close monitoring is recommended. 13. Tafamidis meglumine increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting BCRP in vitro, potentially increasing exposure to BCRP substrates following administration. Dosage adjustments for these substrates may be necessary, and close monitoring is required. 14. Tepotinib increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Alternative drugs should be used if possible. If concomitant use is unavoidable, reduce the P-gp substrate dosage as recommended in its approved product labeling. Close monitoring is essential. 15. Tucatinib increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by inhibiting P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters. Caution is advised, and close monitoring is necessary. Dosage reductions for P-gp substrates should be considered, especially where minimal concentration changes may lead to serious or life-threatening toxicities. 16. Vadadustat increases the levels or effects of tenofovir AF by increasing exposure to BCRP substrates. Caution is required, and close monitoring is recommended. Signs of adverse effects of BCRP substrates should be monitored, and substrate doses should be reduced according to their product labeling. 17. Voclosporin and tenofovir AF may increase each other's toxicity through nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is necessary. Co-administration with drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may increase the risk of acute and/or chronic nephrotoxicity. 18. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommend that HIV-infected mothers should not breastfeed their infants to avoid the risk of postnatal HIV transmission. Emtricitabine (FTC) has been detected in human breast milk, but it is unknown if tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is present in human breast milk. Tenofovir has been found in the milk of lactating rats and rhesus monkeys after administration of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF). It is not known if TAF is present in animal milk. The effects of the drug combination on milk production or breastfed children are also unknown. Due to the potential for HIV transmission (in HIV-negative infants), development of viral resistance (in HIV-positive infants), and adverse reactions in breastfed infants similar to those seen in adults, mothers receiving therapy should be instructed not to breastfeed. 19. Emtricitabine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that, following phosphorylation, interferes with HIV viral DNA polymerase and inhibits viral replication. It is a cytosine analogue. 20. Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) is an NRTI prodrug of tenofovir. Compared to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), TAF is a more targeted form of tenofovir that demonstrates high antiviral efficacy at a dose 10 times lower than TDF, with an improved renal and bone safety profile. It inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by competing with the natural substrate deoxyadenosine 5′-triphosphate and, after incorporation into DNA, by DNA chain termination. 21. TAF can be taken with or without food. It should be stored at 25°C (77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). The container should be tightly closed, and the medication should only be dispensed in its original container. 22.
